council.name: Norwich City Council
council.remit_note: Norwich City Council is a district council with city status. In Norfolk, local government is split between two councils, and Norwich does the half you meet day to day: the council housing it owns and manages itself, bin collections, parks, planning applications, and licensing — who may sell alcohol, put on entertainment, or serve hot food and drink late at night. Roads and potholes, schools and libraries, and social care for children and adults belong to Norfolk County Council instead, so you will not find those here.

topic.name: Council finances
topic.plain_english: Where Norwich City Council's money comes from, what it plans to spend, what it actually spends, and what it owes. It bills you for council tax but keeps only about 13p of every pound: in its own words, "73p going to Norfolk County Council and 14p to the Police and Crime Commissioner". The county's share pays for things like social care and roads. This page is only about the 13p.

questions.asked: Every winter the council asks residents what they think of its budget plans. For 2026/27 it ran a survey from 4 December 2025 to 18 January 2026 and got 899 replies, against a post-2019 average of 1,361. More people opposed the council tax rise than backed it — 48% against, 28% for — and the same survey found 38% unhappy with how the council delivers services against 27% happy. The council published all of it.
questions.decided: Cabinet agreed the budget on 11 February 2026 and full Council set the tax at Budget Council on 24 February. The rise went through at 2.99% — just under the 3% that would have forced a referendum — taking the city's share of a Band D bill to £315.26. Alongside it £313,000 of extra items was put forward, to be paid for from the contingency fund. No minutes of that meeting are in this archive, so we cannot say here how the vote went.
questions.done: Day-to-day spending has come in under budget for five years running, by between 1% and 6.2%. The building programme is a different story: over those same five years the council spent £218.6m of a £342.9m programme, so about a third of the work it approved did not happen in the year it was approved for. Money set aside for emergencies has sat at £8.249m for four year-ends, above the £5.5m floor the council's own finance officer sets.

sources.summary: The external auditor's certificate closing the 2023/24 audit, signed on 1 June 2026. Almost all of it is one finding, carried over from the 2024/25 audit report because it applies to 2023/24 too: a significant weakness in the council's arrangements for overseeing the companies it owns. events.title: The council's own scorecard: 13 green, 2 amber, 4 red
events.summary: Norwich publishes a quarterly performance report with a target and an intervention level for every indicator. For the first quarter of 2025/26, 19 indicators were reported: 13 on or above target, 2 needing attention, and 4 at the level where the council says it will step in.
detail: The four red indicators were the speed of processing new housing benefit claims, the share of council housing rent collected, the time taken to re-let an empty council home, and private-sector insulation measures completed.

One indicator was taken out of the totals this quarter: "The KPI 'Council on track to remain within General Fund Budget' has been removed from the totals for quarter one 2025-2026." The report gives no reason. On a council's own scorecard, that was the indicator for keeping to budget.

The council says of the whole set that "The KPIs in this report have been carried over from the previous Corporate Plan and are under review, as part of the new business planning process." So these are legacy indicators the council is in the middle of replacing.
Two indicators about whether residents feel safe were dropped as well, because the council says they are too heavily influenced by other agencies.
The council explains each red in its own words in the report, and those explanations are carried on this site beside the numbers.

events.title: The council asked residents what they thought of its 2026/27 budget
events.summary: From 4 December 2025 to 18 January 2026 — six and a half weeks — the council ran a survey on its Get Talking Norwich site, promoted by text alert to 120,000 residents. It asked about a 2.99% council tax rise, a new "live budget" reviewed during the year, and a ring-fenced Readiness Fund for the costs of local government reorganisation. 899 people answered, well down on the post-2019 average of 1,361.
detail: More respondents opposed the council tax rise than supported it: 430 of 899 opposed or strongly opposed it and 248 supported it, with 221 neutral — 48% against and 28% for. The 2.99% went through unchanged.

Whether that is a first is something we cannot check from here. Nothing in this archive compares support and opposition across years; the only historical figure the report gives is the response count.
The council states plainly that "no specific factors have been identified to explain the variation in response rate".
Consulting business ratepayers is a legal duty. Consulting residents is the council's own choice.

events.title: Cabinet agreed the 2026/27 budget and a 2.99% council tax rise
events.summary: Cabinet met on 11 February 2026 and agreed a net budget requirement of £24.25m for 2026/27, with a 2.99% rise in the city council's share of council tax. The report printed the consultation result in full, including the answers that did not flatter the council.
detail: The rise stops just under 3%. Above that, a district council has to hold a local referendum: the report says increases are "limited by referendum principles, which for a district council have been set at a maximum of up to 3% for 2026-2027".

The budget requirement rose 16% on the year before, from £20.850m to £24.250m. The council says the settlement replaced its old funding arrangements with a new Fair Funding Allocation, and that its total government funding "increases from £12,970,000 in 2025-2026 to £13,950,000 in 2026-2027, an increase of £980,000".

events.title: The auditors could not give an opinion on the 2024/25 accounts
events.summary: Ernst & Young disclaimed its audit report on the 2024/25 accounts on 23 March 2026: it could not say whether they give a true and fair view. The certificate closing that audit, issued on 17 August 2026, gives no reason for the disclaimer and makes no finding that Norwich's figures are wrong. What the auditor did report, in the certificate for the year before, is a significant weakness in how the council oversees the companies it owns.
detail: The auditor's separate value-for-money work found a significant weakness in governance and in improving economy, efficiency and effectiveness: the council "did not have effective policies, procedures, or governance arrangements for overseeing its part owned and wholly owned subsidiary companies". It found this for 2024/25 and says it applies to 2023/24 as well.

The company in question is Lion Homes (Norwich) Ltd, the council's housing company, which the auditor names among the records it reviewed. The auditor tells the council to rewrite its constitution to cover how it oversees the bodies it owns.
The audit could not be closed until the National Audit Office confirmed it needed no further assurances. That confirmation came, and the certificate was signed on 17 August 2026.

events.title: Over five years the council spent £218.6m of a £342.9m building programme
events.summary: Adding up the capital budget and the capital outturn in each set of accounts from 2021/22 to 2025/26 gives £342.9m approved and £218.6m spent — 64%. The best year was 2024/25 at 79%, the worst 2021/22 at 50%.
detail: Money not spent is not money lost. Most of it rolls into the following year, which is why the in-year capital budget keeps growing: by the 2025/26 year end the capital budget stood at £94.768m.
It does mean the published capital programme is not a reliable statement of what will actually be built next year.
The budget figure used here is the revised in-year budget, which is the right basis for comparing delivery but is a target that had already been re-set once.

events.title: The 2025/26 accounts: £0.710m under on services, £38.3m of building work not done
events.summary: The draft accounts for 2025/26 report a General Fund underspend of £0.710m — 1.03% of the gross General Fund expenditure budget — and a Housing Revenue Account underspend of £4.223m, 5.08%. Capital spending was £56.477m against a budget of £94.768m, so £38.291m of approved building work did not happen that year.
detail: The council names £1.286m of interest on its day-to-day cash as contributing to a £2.992m underspend in Corporate Financing, the central pot.

Everything outside that central pot went over budget by £2.282m, and the central pot covered it. Something similar happened in each of the two years before, at very different scale: £2.011m in 2023/24, and £118,000 in 2024/25, which on a budget of about £65m is a rounding error, and in that year three of the four service areas underspent.
The accounts are draft, which means the external auditor has not signed them off.

measures.label: Borrowing against the limits full Council set, 2025/26
measures.rule: Green if the council's reported figure met or beat the target it set itself. The operational boundary is the level it expects to work within — £314.409m for 2025/26 — and the authorised limit is the legal ceiling it may not pass, £344.409m. Against them the council puts its external borrowing at £145.948m, well inside both. Nearly all of it is Public Works Loan Board money, government lending at government rates. Borrowing far below a ceiling is not by itself good or bad: the ceiling is a limit, not something to aim at.

promises.council_caveat: Local government reorganisation is the national programme that may abolish Norwich City Council and fold it into a larger authority. Every forecast the council publishes beyond 2026/27 carries that caveat, put there by the council itself.
promises.evidence: The council's budget report describes "The proposed Readiness Fund, a ring-fenced fund to manage in-year financial pressures, including costs associated with Local Government Reorganisation and inflation". That is a proposal in the report Cabinet put forward, not a record of what full Council finally agreed — the only Budget Council document in this archive is the council tax resolution, which does not cover it. Whether the fund exists, and what it was spent on, will not be visible until the year's accounts are published in summer 2027.

promises.question: Did the extra £313,000 councillors voted for get spent on what they voted for?
promises.label: £313,000 for enforcement, communal areas and community clean-ups
promises.rule: Green if a later council record confirms it was done by that date. Amber if a later record shows it was done late, or only partly. Red if a later record says it was not done. Grey if no later council record mentions it — which means the promise cannot be checked, not that it was broken.

target.display: "Investments in enforcement to deliver visible improvements… Communal areas improvements… Community clean-up activity… 313" — Annex C, Budget Council, 24 February 2026

promises.council_caveat: The council built its own check into the promise: "A six-month review will assess progress against KPIs and consider whether targeted community-action pilots… should be incorporated where evidence shows additional benefit."
promises.evidence: Annex C to the Budget Council papers for 24 February 2026 lists £313,000 of extra spending — fly-tipping and graffiti enforcement, bin stores and recycling in flats, community clean-ups, and political assistants — to be funded "in-year from the 2026-2027 budget contingency". The annex says this part "will form part of the substantive motion and not as an amendment", so it was in the budget put to the vote rather than tabled against it. The same annex carries amendments from the other groups that were not part of that motion: £65,000 for a ward-level community cohesion fund from the Green and Liberal Democrat groups, and £45,000 for tree planting and £55,000 for river education from the Green group. No minute of that meeting is in this archive, so we cannot say from here what was finally agreed, or what has been spent since.

gaps.description: Accounts before 2021/22. The council publishes them back to 2018/19 and they are linked from the same page, but each set is a large file and this archive stops at 2021/22 to keep the repository a reasonable size. The earlier years can be read on the council's own site.

What the wind-up of the council's housing company finally cost. Lion Homes (Norwich) Ltd could not repay £6.15m of loans that fell due on 31 March 2025 and went into a members' voluntary liquidation. The 2024/25 accounts say the council "has impaired the total amount of the loans to nil" and cut the value of its shareholding from £3.424m to £2.825m. The external auditor's finding on how the company came to be so little watched is on the record — "Based on the evidence available, there is no indication that adequate oversight arrangements for subsidiaries have ever existed, dating back to the subsidiary's incorporation in November 2015" — but no published document gives a final cost, and we will not publish an estimate of one.

Whether the savings the council promises each February are actually made by the following March. The council publishes the savings it has identified when it sets the budget — £3.2m for 2025/26, £3.1m for 2024/25 — but no outturn report or set of accounts we have read tracks delivery against them as a single figure. This is the most obvious accountability question about a council's money, and it cannot be answered from Norwich's published papers. It is a fair question for a resident to put to the council directly.

Why some of the council's own indicators are not on this page. Its quarter one 2025/26 report says "There are 20 quarterly KPIs reported for this period" and its totals table counts 19, alongside a handful of annual indicators reported once a year. This site carries eighteen of them, picked because each answers a question about money, about a target the council set itself, or about a service a resident uses. Eight are on the same dashboard and are not here: household waste recycled, food premises inspected, planning appeals, planning applications decided in time, underused council land, CO2 reduction, and two on IT availability. We have not published a rule for that choice, so the count of greens, ambers and reds on this page cannot be set against the council's own count. The council also says of every one of these indicators that "The KPIs in this report have been carried over from the previous Corporate Plan and are under review, as part of the new business planning process."

Why the 2024/25 audit opinion was disclaimed. The certificate says only that Ernst & Young could not give an opinion and that the audit was later closed once the National Audit Office confirmed it needed nothing further. It gives no reason. A disclaimed opinion has been common across English councils since the government set deadlines to clear a national audit backlog, and that context matters to reading this one — but no council document in this archive says so, so this page does not say it either. What we looked for: an explanation in the council's own published audit papers. What is not banked here: the Annual Governance Statements, and any national guidance on the audit backlog.

A published target for most of the money on this page. Norwich sets targets for its corporate performance indicators, but not for how close its spending should come to budget, how much of its building programme it should deliver, or how much of its income should come from commercial property. Those measures are scored against the council's own plan rather than a target, using rules published on the methodology page, and the commercial income one cannot be scored at all.

How much the council's government funding has risen or fallen in real terms since 2019/20. Answering that needs the government's Core Spending Power tables for each year, which are national statistics rather than council papers and are not in this archive. Without them we can show what the council received but not what it is worth. It is the single most-asked question about council finances and we cannot answer it yet.

Performance figures in a form anyone can check. Norwich publishes a full set of targets and actuals every quarter, which is more than many district councils manage. But the numbers live in Appendix A of the report as screenshots of a dashboard, not as text or a spreadsheet, so they cannot be searched, copied or checked by machine. Every target measure on this site was read off those images by eye. The council also runs a live Power BI dashboard on its website, which is a JavaScript embed and cannot be archived either.
